# How This Book Is Written {.unnumbered}

A book about AI-native engineering should practice what it teaches. I am writing this synthesis during an academic sabbatical at Harvard University while spending dedicated time at ETH Zürich, with the goal of bringing a fully polished volume to completion by the end of 2027. Releasing early drafts in the open creates a powerful form of personal accountability. Working with generative AI systems every day exposes both their practical utility and their failure modes.

The basis for this book grew out of our initial paper on Architecture 2.0 [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. Bringing computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation together into a coherent framework required years of work across three distinct communities. Each of these fields operates under different physical constraints and evidence standards, and bridging them demands far more than a clever prompt.

Because this monograph explores AI-native systems, I built an AI-native authoring engine to write it. I treat generative models as an expansive information vault to explore design alternatives, examine interdisciplinary literature, and surface historical connections efficiently. To maintain technical rigor, I structure the authoring workflow around specialized review roles. Simulated learner panels evaluate pedagogical clarity, senior architect panels test technical bounds, systems panels inspect tool interfaces, and citation auditors verify evidence. As shown in @fig-author-ai-workflow, these review roles feed directly into an automated build harness that compiles the manuscript and validates formatting.

![**The AI-native authoring engine operates as an out-of-order multi-agent design loop.** Backward design establishes intent first. The generation swarm communicates across a shared inter-agent bus to propose drafts, while simulated review panels supply critique. The human author in the central hub functions with in-order commit authority over what reaches the deterministic validation harness. System architects will recognize a structural parallelism to a modern out-of-order CPU datapath: Stage 1 acts as frontend fetch and decode, the agent swarms act as parallel execution units, and the central author hub acts as the reorder buffer and commit stage holding 100% retirement authority.](images/fig-author-ai-workflow.svg){#fig-author-ai-workflow width="100%" fig-alt="Architecture diagram showing Stage 1 Backward Design, Stage 2 Human-in-the-Loop Core and Simulated Agent Review Panels, Stage 3 Validation Harness."}

Operating an AI-native authoring engine rapidly demonstrates that generation velocity is not synthesis quality. In an early draft, an agent swarm produced thirty pages of fluent prose on hardware-software co-design in under two minutes. On close inspection, however, the text subtly blurred the line between cycle-accurate simulation and physical signoff gates, offering smooth generalities where hard engineering trade-offs belonged. Rebuilding that chapter required hours of pruning back to first principles. Generative models produce candidate options, but human supervision and engineering judgment govern every decision that reaches the page. As the author, I decide which distinctions matter, what the evidence supports, where an analogy fails, and what must be cut.

Developing the manuscript alongside runnable reference code keeps these principles grounded in executable reality. While the manuscript and reference code are developed in the open, I keep the internal prompt orchestrations, subagent configurations, and rule files private. Just as a chip design team open-sources reference RTL while guarding internal PDK flows and physical design scripts, the engineering value lies in how the machinery is governed to enforce rigor.

Writing is how I test whether I truly understand a subject well enough to teach it. When an explanation cannot survive a reader's questions, the synthesis is not finished. This remains a working manuscript, and I welcome your feedback. If you spot a flaw, an imprecise claim, or a trade-off that needs a harder test, please reach out to me directly.

Vijay Janapa Reddi
*Harvard University / ETH Zürich*
